Nevertheless
nĕv-er-thē-lĕs´
adv. (notwithstanding; rendering Greek plen and de)
Never-the-less: not the less for all that. The Bible's great hinge-word, on which prayers, obediences, and Gethsemane itself turn.

Biblical Definition

Nevertheless concedes everything and surrenders nothing. Peter's empty nets: “Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net” (Luk 5:5). Asaph's envy-sick heart: “Nevertheless I am continually with thee” (Psa 73:23). The apostasy of professors: “Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure” (2Ti 2:19). And the darkest garden in history: “nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” (Luk 22:42). Faith's grammar lives in this adverb — the facts admitted, the obedience anyway.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines nevertheless as not the less; notwithstanding; that is, in opposition to any thing, or without regarding it.

expand to see more

NEVERTHELESS, adv. Not the less; notwithstanding; that is, in opposition to any thing, or without regarding it.

Key Scripture

Luk 5:5 — "And Simon answering said unto him, Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net."

Psa 73:23 — "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand."

2Ti 2:19 — "Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity."

Luk 22:42 — "Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done."

Modern Corruption

Positivity culture forbids the first half of the word (admit nothing negative) and autonomy culture forbids the second (submit to nothing anyway) — between them, the hinge of faith rusts unused.

expand to see more

Every nevertheless has two chambers: an honest concession and an overriding commitment. Modern religious optimism amputates the concession — toil-all-night-and-take-nothing must be reframed, never admitted — producing a faith that cannot survive an honest bad night. Peter's obedience is stronger precisely because his report is bleak: all night, nothing. Faith is not the refusal to count empty nets; it is letting down the net after counting them, at His word.

Gethsemane spends the word's full price. The cup is really dreaded; the if-it-be-possible is really prayed; and then the hinge turns: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done. Every lesser surrender borrows from that one. A generation catechized to treat its own will as sacred has lost the word's second chamber — and with it, the only prayer that ever carried a soul through a garden at night.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek plen (G4133), howbeit, but, nevertheless — the adversative that turns Gethsemane; elsewhere simple de carries the same holy pivot.

expand to see more

Greek plen (G4133) — but, nevertheless, notwithstanding; Luke 22:42, and rejoice not that the spirits are subject unto you, but rather rejoice… (Luk 10:20).

Usage

"“Nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net” — the facts counted, the obedience anyway."

"“Nevertheless I am continually with thee” — the psalm turns from envy to presence on one adverb."

"“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” — the hinge on which redemption swung."
